stages.title: Millions of shoppers, one shop
stages.desc: Millions of shoppers, one shop, one physical building. Logins, carts and checkouts all land on that same single server.

stages.title: Everything depends on that one box
stages.desc: The traditional design: users, one app server, one database, all in one datacenter. No spare copy exists anywhere else.

stages.title: Maintenance starts. The server goes offline
stages.desc: A patch, a reboot, a failed power supply, a fibre cut — it does not matter which. The one box simply stops answering requests.

stages.title: Customers cannot log in
stages.desc: The architecture diagram never showed a single point of failure — but your customer sees a spinner, then a timeout, then leaves.

stages.title: This is what the outage costs
stages.desc: Lost checkouts, refunded orders, a support queue and a damaged reputation — the bill keeps growing for every minute the box reboots.

stages.title: Azure splits a region into zones
stages.desc: Every zone-enabled Azure region has three or more physically separate datacenters, each with its own power, cooling and network path.

stages.title: Run the shop in all three
stages.desc: One zone-redundant load balancer in front, an app instance in every zone, and the database in a zone-redundant configuration across all three.

stages.title: Zones share data synchronously
stages.desc: Under 2 ms apart, close enough that a write can wait for all three. The commit only acknowledges once every zone has confirmed it — zero data loss.

stages.title: Zone 2 fails. The shop stays open
stages.desc: The load balancer's health probe stops sending traffic there within seconds. Zones 1 and 3 absorb the load — logins keep working uninterrupted.

stages.title: One server: 99.9%. Three zones: 99.99%
stages.desc: Azure backs single-zone at 99.9% and zone-redundant at 99.99% — 8.7 hours of allowed downtime a year becomes 52 minutes.

end.title: One zone can burn. Your shop keeps selling
end.sub: Azure Availability Zones: three physically separate datacenters in one region, under 2 ms apart, so a whole building can fail without a single customer noticing.

post.caption:
A shopping app with millions of users. One server. Maintenance starts, the box goes offline, and nobody can log in.

That outage is not a technical event. It is lost customers, lost revenue and screenshots of your error page living on social media long after the server is back.

Azure Availability Zones fix it at the architecture level. Every zone-enabled region is three or more physically separate datacenters, each with its own power, cooling and network, under 2 ms apart. Put an instance in each one, front them with a zone-redundant load balancer, replicate the database across them — and a whole datacenter can fail mid-checkout while zones 1 and 3 absorb the traffic.

That 2 ms is the whole trick. Zones are close enough to replicate synchronously: the write goes to all three, and the commit is only acknowledged once every zone has it. Lose a zone and there is nothing to recover. RPO zero. Across regions the latency is far too high to wait for, so that replication is asynchronous and failover costs you data.

Which is also the catch: your app instances share nothing. Session state in a web server’s memory dies with its zone. Move state into zone-redundant services — ZRS storage, a zone-redundant database, zone-redundant Redis — or a third of your customers get logged out anyway.

The SLA follows the design: 99.9% for a single VM, 99.99% for two or more spread across zones. 8.7 hours of downtime a year, or 52 minutes.
